doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

chapter: Views on drummers and the state of jazz
title: Race in jazz and young musicians
summary: He says he sees people as people, and discusses experimentation by younger players that record companies will not release.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Good statement. It’s home grown. Have you experienced any kind of, or witnessed any racial scene in jazz that you find significant?

I have a friend who’s a drummer. He happens to be a person of color, and I don’t even like to say that to be honest with you because I look at people as people and I’ve never met a man I don’t like, Will Rogers. It’s however they act and treat me that will judge that in the end. But I’ve been in situations where I’ve gone to clubs that were predominantly black and I just don’t have that attitude so they don’t give me that attitude. My friend is a person of color and he’s like one of my best friends. And we share jobs, anxieties, I just look — there’s four people up on the bandstand and that’s how I look at it. And I’ve never been in a situation with musicians — maybe at first there might be some apprehension on their part, but as soon as they hear me play it dissolves and we have a great gig.

From what I’ve been able to observe it seems like there’s a healthy group of fairly young musicians who are keeping the let’s say mainstream tradition alive, kind of a little resurgence with Scott Hamilton there, but it doesn’t seem like there’s as many young black musicians who are embracing that style, that they seem to be devoted more towards really kind of modern.

Well we could talk about that. I think that what you’re saying is partially true about them keeping the roots of bebop alive, but I hear experimentation from some younger players, I mean get into that. Maybe what they’re coming up with isn’t commercially viable or marketable and so we don’t really hear it. But as far as experimentation going on, certainly. But whether we can get record producers to get it out there is a big problem, and we may not be hearing some of the next steps to jazz or to modern music to fusion because simply I don’t think the record companies want to take a chance. They want the sure thing. They want the already-established name to come out with the CD where they can project record, CD sales. So I think the experimentation is going on. I hear it with college groups, writers, but it’s not getting out there and I think it’s really something that needs to be addressed.
